title: Different loves
hookLine: agape, bhakti, metta, ishq, ren: not one love under many names, but many loves

cards: Five words, from five places. Agape. Bhakti.

A greeting card could print them in a circle around a heart and call them all love, in five languages. A lovely card, and maybe a wrong one. Put them back where they came from, and they pull in different directions.
One gives without waiting to be earned. One sings to God. One wishes well to every living being.

teach.h: AGAPE: THE GIFT, EVEN TO THE ENEMY.
teach.b: Agape first. It's a Greek word the New Testament uses for love, and in First Corinthians the King James Bible renders it charity: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind.”
It's love as a gift, and in the Gospels Jesus stretches it as far as the enemy. Agape points outward, to the neighbor and the stranger. Bhakti is Sanskrit.
In Hindu devotion it means loving God personally, with the whole heart, and in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the devoted one is dear to him.
Bhakti points toward a Beloved with a name and a face. Metta is Pali, from the Buddhist teachings, often put into English as loving-kindness.
In the Metta Sutta the image is a mother guarding her only child, and that care is stretched toward all beings, without limit. It asks nothing back.

teach.h: ISHQ AND REN: BURNING, AND HOME.
teach.b: Ishq is a word Sufi poets use for a love that burns and won't stay polite. Rumi calls love the astrolabe of God's mysteries. Ishq points toward the One, and it aches.
Ren is Chinese, from Confucius, often rendered humaneness. Asked about it, Confucius answers: love people. And the Analects say being a good son and a good brother is its root.
Ren starts at home and grows outward through duties. So here's the turn. These aren't five names for one feeling.
They differ in who is loved, what is asked, and where it starts.
Metta wishes all beings well; ren begins with your own parents. Bhakti longs for one Beloved; agape reaches the enemy. Each word means most inside its own tradition.
One English word flattens them. Keeping them apart is a way of honoring each.

how: Each tradition keeps its own word: Christians speak of agape, Hindu devotees express bhakti in song and worship, Buddhists practice metta toward all beings, Sufi poets write of ishq, and Confucian teaching roots ren in family duty.

games.q: a friend says every tradition means the same thing by love. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: yes, it's one love with many names.
the words differ in who is loved and what is asked.
love can't be talked about at all.
games.why: agape reaches the enemy, metta wishes all beings well, ren starts at home: real differences, and none ranked.

practice: Let the five pass slowly through your mind, like faces in a crowd: agape, the gift that reaches the stranger; bhakti, devotion to the divine; metta, goodwill to every being; ishq, the longing that burns; ren, care that starts at home.
Notice which one stays; there's no right answer. When it's clear, name it silently. If you pray, you can hold that love in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Different loves. Five words from five traditions, each pointing its own way: not one love under many names, but many loves. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from the New Testament: love as a gift, toward neighbor and enemy.
